title: Develop a production and strategic plan for the agricultural business

lessons.title: Strategic planning for the farm business
lessons.html:
Where are we going and how will we get there?

A strategic plan sets the long-term direction of the agricultural business, usually for three to ten years. A production plan translates that direction into what will be produced each season. Together they guide investment, enterprise choices and daily management.

Elements of a strategic plan

  1. Vision: what the business wants to become (e.g. 'a leading supplier of export-quality citrus from the Sundays River Valley').
  2. Mission: what the business does, for whom and how.
  3. Values: principles such as safety, fairness, sustainability.
  4. Situation analysis: internal (resources, skills, finances) and external (markets, climate, policy, competitors).
  5. Strategic goals and measurable objectives.
  6. Strategies to achieve them.
  7. Action plans, budgets and responsibilities.
  8. Monitoring and review.

Analysis tools

  • SWOT: strengths, weaknesses (internal), opportunities, threats (external).
  • PESTLE: political, economic, social, technological, legal and environmental factors, for example exchange rates, interest rates, load-shedding, land reform policy, labour law changes, climate variability.
  • Benchmarking: compare yields, costs and margins with study groups or industry figures.

Strategic choices

Typical choices include: grow or consolidate, specialise or diversify, move up the value chain (packing, processing), change markets (local to export), adopt new technology, or partner with others. Each choice must be tested against resources, risks and the owners' goals.

lessons.title: Developing the production plan
lessons.html:
From strategy to the field

The production plan states what will be produced, where, when, how much and with what inputs. It covers one season or year and is updated each cycle.

Steps

  1. Resource allocation: assign land units, water, buildings and machinery to enterprises.
  2. Enterprise budgets: for each crop or livestock enterprise, estimate yield, price, income and variable costs to calculate the gross margin.
  3. Production calendar: soil preparation, planting, fertilising, spraying, irrigation, breeding, weaning, harvesting and marketing dates.
  4. Input plan: quantities and timing of seed, fertiliser, chemicals, feed, remedies and fuel.
  5. Labour plan: permanent and seasonal requirements by month.
  6. Machinery plan: capacity, maintenance and contractor needs.
  7. Cash flow budget: monthly income and expenses to show financing needs.

Example gross margin

Item (per ha, dryland maize)Example R
Income: 5 t × R3 500/t17 500
Seed, fertiliser, chemicals8 000
Fuel, repairs, contractors3 000
Insurance, marketing, other variable1 500
Gross margin5 000

Figures are illustrative only; use your own records and current prices. Test the budget with sensitivity analysis: what if yield is 3,5 t or the price is R3 000?

Risk planning

Include contingencies: crop insurance, drought fodder reserves, alternative markets, backup power for irrigation, and biosecurity plans for disease outbreaks.

lessons.title: Implementing, monitoring and reviewing plans
lessons.html:
Making plans happen

Turning plans into action

  • Break strategic goals into annual objectives and quarterly milestones.
  • Assign each action to a person with a deadline.
  • Communicate the plan to managers, supervisors and staff so everyone understands their part.
  • Align budgets with the plan: money follows priorities.

Key performance indicators

AreaKPI examples
ProductionYield per ha, calving %, kg weaned per cow
FinancialGross margin per ha, cost per unit, return on assets, debt ratio
MarketAverage price vs market, % top grade
PeopleLost-time injuries, staff turnover, training hours
ResourcesWater use per tonne, ground cover

Monitoring cycle

Compare actual results with the plan monthly (cash flow, production records) and quarterly (KPIs). When results deviate, ask why: was it weather, management, market or a wrong assumption? Decide on corrective actions.

Review

At the end of each season hold a formal review of the production plan. Review the strategic plan every year, and rewrite it when the environment changes significantly, for example after a major drought, a market loss or a change of ownership. Include family members and key staff in reviews, and consider succession planning in family businesses.

Financing the plan

Present the strategic and production plans with budgets to banks or financiers. A well-documented plan with realistic assumptions improves access to credit and terms.

Key points

  • A strategic plan sets long-term direction; a production plan sets seasonal actions.
  • Use SWOT, PESTLE and benchmarking for analysis.
  • Base the production plan on enterprise gross margins, calendars and cash flow.
  • Test budgets with sensitivity analysis and plan for risks.
  • Monitor KPIs and review plans regularly.
